uses: The part used is the fleshy red calyx that cups each seed pod. Steeped, it makes a tart, deep red drink enjoyed in many countries, and in the Caribbean a festive version is served at Christmas. The drink is popularly taken for high blood pressure, a use now tested in clinical trials, and in some cultures it is taken by nursing mothers in the hope of more milk. The calyces also go into jams, sauces, syrups and wine, the leaves are cooked as a tangy green, and the stems give a strong fiber.
caution_pregnancy: No source we read establishes that hibiscus is safe in medicinal amounts during pregnancy, and human studies are lacking. Not enough is known; avoid it beyond ordinary drink amounts. For breastfeeding, there are no data on whether it passes into milk or on its safety for nursing babies, and no good trials show it increases milk.
caution_medications: Hibiscus can lower blood pressure, so if you take blood pressure medicines, ask your prescriber first. In animal studies it raised and prolonged blood levels of the water pill hydrochlorothiazide and increased urine output; whether this happens in people isn't known. A 2020 review found few clinically important interactions at normal amounts.
caution_conditions: If you have low blood pressure, take care, since hibiscus can lower it further. Allergic reactions are possible, including in people sensitive to other mallow-family plants such as marshmallow. In rats, very high amounts were linked to raised liver enzymes and uric acid.
caution_duration: Our sources set no time limit and report no long-term studies. If you drink it for blood pressure, keep your doctor informed.
caution_topical: Our sources don't cover putting hibiscus on the skin, so not enough is known about skin use.
garden_harvest_timing: Pick the calyces while plump and tender, before they turn brown, in autumn as the days shorten; picking encourages more buds. Separate them from the seed pods before use.
garden_sun: Full sun; will not grow in shade
garden_water: Well-drained soil; water when rain is short. Deep roots make it fairly drought tolerant
notes: Native to Central and West Africa; a relative of okra. NC State's plant database now files it under a new name, Sabdariffa gossypiifolia. It needs a long, warm season and flowers only when nights grow long, so in cool climates grow it as an annual and expect a late or small harvest. Frost kills it. Root-knot nematodes are its main pest; rotate where you plant it.
